lessonTitle: Buoyancy and the Grashof and Rayleigh Numbers

blocks.text: Above a hot radiator panel a visible shimmer of air rises smoothly for the first few centimetres, then starts to flicker and break up. No fan is involved: buoyancy alone drives the flow, and the same dimensionless number decides when it turns turbulent.

blocks.markdown: In **natural (free) convection** the fluid moves because density differences, created by temperature differences, produce a buoyancy force. Warm fluid next to a hot wall is lighter than the cool fluid farther away, so it rises, drawing in cool fluid at the base. There is no imposed velocity, so there is no Reynolds number: buoyancy takes its place, and we characterise the flow with the Grashof and Rayleigh numbers.

blocks.title: Volumetric expansion coefficient
blocks.text: $\beta=-\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial T}\right)_p$ (K$^{-1}$) measures how much density falls per unit temperature rise. For an ideal gas $\rho=p/(RT)$ so $\beta=1/T$, with $T$ the absolute temperature in kelvin, usually the film temperature $T_f=(T_s+T_\infty)/2$. For liquids $\beta$ is taken from property tables.

blocks.markdown: The buoyant force per unit volume on warm fluid is about $\rho g\beta\Delta T$. This is opposed by viscous drag in the boundary layer. The ratio of buoyancy to viscous forces is the **Grashof number**. Since heat is spread by thermal diffusion at the same time, the product of $Gr$ and $Pr$, the **Rayleigh number**, controls the flow and heat transfer.

blocks.caption: g = 9.81 m/s^2; L the vertical height (m); nu kinematic viscosity, alpha thermal diffusivity (m^2/s), properties at the film temperature

blocks.title: Rayleigh number of a heated vertical plate
blocks.prompt: A vertical plate 0.6 m tall is held at 70 $^\circ$C in still air at 20 $^\circ$C. Use air properties at the film temperature (typical): $\nu=1.8\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s and thermal diffusivity $\alpha=2.5\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s. Find the Grashof and Rayleigh numbers and say whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent.

steps.text: Film temperature $T_f=(70+20)/2=45$ $^\circ$C $=318.15$ K. For an ideal gas the volumetric expansion coefficient is $\beta=1/T_f=0.00314$ K$^{-1}$ (with $T$ in kelvin).
Compare with the transition value $Ra_L\approx10^9$ for a vertical plate: $Ra_L=7.40e+08$ is below it, so the boundary layer is laminar.

blocks.answer: $Gr_L\approx1.03e+09$ and $Ra_L\approx7.40e+08$, so the flow is laminar ($Ra_L<10^9$).

blocks.caption: Dimensionless groups for natural convection

blocks.markdown: For a vertical plate the boundary layer starts laminar at the bottom and thickens upward. It turns turbulent when $Ra_x=g\beta\Delta Tx^3/(\nu\alpha)$ reaches about $10^9$, where $x$ is the distance up the plate. Because $Ra\propto x^3$, the transition point is reached quickly with height and tall surfaces are partly turbulent. For $Ra_L<10^9$ the whole layer is laminar.

blocks.title: Why a tall wall goes turbulent
blocks.prompt: A tall room wall of height 2.5 m is 10 K warmer than the room air at a film temperature of about 300 K. Use $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s and $\alpha=2.25\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s (typical). Find $Ra_L$ at the top of the wall and the height at which the flow is expected to turn turbulent.

steps.text: This exceeds $10^9$, so the layer becomes turbulent somewhere up the wall. Since $Ra_x\propto x^3$, the transition height is $x_t=L(10^9/Ra_L)^{1/3}=2.5\times(0.0705)^{1/3}=1.03$ m.
For comparison, a wall half as tall (1.25 m) has $Ra_L=1.77e+09$, which is 8 times smaller because $Ra\propto L^3$, though it still exceeds $10^9$, so its upper part would also be turbulent.

blocks.answer: $Ra_L\approx1.4e+10$; transition at about 1.03 m, so the upper part of the wall has a turbulent boundary layer.

items: Convert temperatures to kelvin and find $T_f=(T_s+T_\infty)/2$.
Find $\beta=1/T_f$ for a gas; find $\nu$, $\alpha$ (or $Pr$) at $T_f$.
Choose the characteristic length $L$: height for a vertical surface.
Compare $Ra_L$ with $10^9$ to decide laminar versus turbulent.

blocks.title: Kelvin and length
blocks.text: Using $\beta=1/T$ with temperatures in $^\circ$C is a frequent error that gives results that are several times too large (e.g. $1/45$ instead of $1/318$). The length enters as $L^3$, so a small error in $L$ is amplified; always check units (m, not mm).

blocks.title: Natural convection scaling
blocks.text: $Ra\propto\Delta T\,L^3$: doubling $\Delta T$ doubles $Ra$; doubling the height multiplies $Ra$ by eight. Higher $T_f$ lowers $\beta$ for a gas, which weakens buoyancy. The laminar-to-turbulent transition in free convection occurs at $Ra\approx10^9$ on a vertical plate.

points: Natural convection is driven by buoyancy: $\beta=1/T$ for an ideal gas (with $T$ in kelvin).
On a vertical plate the boundary layer is laminar for $Ra_L<10^9$ and becomes turbulent near $Ra\approx10^9$.
$Ra\propto L^3\Delta T$, so size and temperature difference strongly affect the flow regime.

questions.stem: For an ideal gas at absolute temperature $T$ (in kelvin) the volumetric expansion coefficient is

distractorRationale.b: The units are wrong: $\beta$ has units K$^{-1}$.
distractorRationale.c: The ideal gas law needs absolute temperature; using $^\circ$C gives a wrong, much larger value.

questions.explanation: From $\rho=p/(RT)$ at constant pressure, $\beta=-(1/\rho)(\partial\rho/\partial T)_p=1/T$. The temperature must be absolute because the ideal gas law is written for kelvin.

questions.stem: For natural convection on a vertical heated plate, the boundary layer is expected to change from laminar to turbulent when the Rayleigh number based on height is about

distractorRationale.a: At $Ra$ near $10^3$ the layer is laminar and buoyancy is weak.
distractorRationale.c: This is the transition Reynolds number for a pipe, not a Rayleigh number.
distractorRationale.d: This is the transition Reynolds number for a flat plate in forced flow.

questions.explanation: The free-convection boundary layer on a vertical plate becomes turbulent near $Ra_x\approx10^9$. Pipe and plate values for $Re$ belong to forced flows.

questions.stem: Air in a hot oven is at 87 $^\circ$C. Treating it as an ideal gas, find the volumetric expansion coefficient $\beta$ in K$^{-1}$.
questions.explanation: $\beta=1/T$ with $T=87+273.15=360.15$ K, so $\beta=0.002777$ K$^{-1}$. Using Celsius would give 0.0115 K$^{-1}$, about four times too large.

questions.stem: A vertical plate 0.35 m tall is at 60 $^\circ$C in air at 20 $^\circ$C. At the film temperature of 313.15 K, $\nu=1.7\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s and $\alpha=2.4\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s (typical). Find $Ra_L$ in units of $10^8$ (i.e. enter 1.32 for $1.32\times10^8$).
questions.explanation: $\beta=1/313.15$ K$^{-1}$, so $Ra_L=9.81\times(1/313.15)\times40\times0.35^3/(1.7\times10^{-5}\times2.4\times10^{-5})=1.317e+08$. This is below $10^9$, so the boundary layer is laminar.

questions.stem: A vertical rod of height 0.20 m at 100 $^\circ$C stands in air at 20 $^\circ$C. Take $T_f=333.15$ K and $\nu=1.95\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s. Find the Grashof number $Gr_L$ in units of $10^7$ (enter 4.96 for $4.96\times10^7$).
questions.explanation: $\beta=1/333.15=0.00300$ K$^{-1}$ and $\Delta T=80$ K. $Gr_L=9.81\times0.00300\times80\times0.2^3/(1.95\times10^{-5})^2=4.956e+07$. Multiplying by $Pr\approx0.71$ would give $Ra_L$.

questions.stem: A natural convection layer has $Ra_L$ for a vertical plate of height $L$. If the plate is replaced by a taller one of height $2L$ at the same $\Delta T$ and fluid, the Rayleigh number becomes

distractorRationale.a: $L$ appears cubed in $Ra$, not to the first power.
distractorRationale.b: $L^2$ would apply to an area; $Ra$ has $L^3$.
distractorRationale.c: That would be $L^4$, which does not appear in the definition.

questions.explanation: $Ra_L=g\beta\Delta TL^3/(\nu\alpha)\propto L^3$, so doubling the height multiplies $Ra$ by $2^3=8$. This is why tall surfaces become turbulent far more readily than short ones.

questions.stem: A wall 1.5 m tall at 35 $^\circ$C in air at 15 $^\circ$C has (using $T_f=298$ K, $\nu=1.6\times10^{-5}$ and $\alpha=2.25\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s) $Ra_L\approx6.17\times10^9$. The boundary layer is

options.text: laminar over the whole wall, since $Ra_L$ is large
laminar, because natural convection is always laminar
turbulent over the upper part of the wall, since $Ra_L$ exceeds $10^9$
fully turbulent from the bottom edge, since $Ra_L>10^9$

questions.correctOptionText: turbulent over the upper part of the wall, since $Ra_L$ exceeds $10^9$

distractorRationale.a: A large $Ra$ above $10^9$ indicates transition; laminar flow exists only below it.
distractorRationale.b: Natural convection can become turbulent on tall surfaces.
distractorRationale.d: The layer starts laminar at the leading edge and turns turbulent only where $Ra_x$ reaches $10^9$.

questions.explanation: $Ra_L=6.172e+09>10^9$, so the layer starts laminar at the base and becomes turbulent at the height where $Ra_x=10^9$, i.e. $x\approx0.82$ m.

questions.stem: Describe the physical reason natural convection boundary layers on a vertical surface transition from laminar to turbulent flow and explain why the transition is expressed in terms of the Rayleigh number rather than the Reynolds number.
markingGuide: Buoyancy accelerates the fluid up the wall, so the layer thickens and the local velocity grows with height.
Instabilities (disturbances) grow when buoyancy is strong relative to damping by viscosity and thermal diffusion, which is measured by $Ra_x=g\beta\Delta Tx^3/(\nu\alpha)$.
There is no free-stream velocity, so a Reynolds number cannot be built from an imposed flow; $Ra$ (or $Gr$) takes its place.
Transition occurs at $Ra_x\approx10^9$ on a vertical plate, and $Ra\propto x^3$ so tall surfaces become turbulent.
questions.explanation: The reasoning is that buoyancy drives the flow, so buoyancy-to-damping ratios are the right dimensionless controls. The transition value is empirical.

questions.stem: Show that the volumetric expansion coefficient of an ideal gas is $\beta=1/T$. Hence explain how the strength of natural convection (for a given $\Delta T$ and fluid properties) changes when the film temperature rises from 300 K to 600 K, and what other property changes also matter.
markingGuide: From $\rho=p/(RT)$: $\partial\rho/\partial T=-p/(RT^2)=-\rho/T$ at constant $p$, so $\beta=-(1/\rho)(\partial\rho/\partial T)=1/T$.
Doubling $T_f$ from 300 K to 600 K halves $\beta$, which halves the buoyancy for the same $\Delta T$ and lowers $Ra$.
In gases $\nu$ and $\alpha$ increase strongly with temperature (roughly with $T^{1.7}$ to $T^{1.8}$), so $\nu\alpha$ in the denominator rises much faster than $\beta$ falls, further reducing $Ra$.
The net effect is a much smaller $Ra$ at the higher temperature for the same $\Delta T$ and $L$.
questions.explanation: The derivation uses the ideal gas law at constant pressure. The effect of temperature on $\nu$ and $\alpha$ is stronger than that on $\beta$, so high-temperature gas has a lower Rayleigh number for fixed size and $\Delta T$.

questions.stem: The side wall of an electrical cabinet is 1.2 m tall at 55 $^\circ$C in still air at 25 $^\circ$C. At the film temperature $T_f=313.15$ K, $\nu=1.7\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s and $\alpha=2.4\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s (typical). Find $Ra_L$ in units of $10^9$ (enter 3.98 for $3.98\times10^9$); then state whether the layer is fully laminar.
questions.explanation: $\beta=1/313.15$ K$^{-1}$, so $Ra_L=9.81\times(1/313.15)\times30\times1.2^3/(1.7\times10^{-5}\times2.4\times10^{-5})=3.980e+09$. This is above $10^9$, so the layer is not fully laminar; turbulence sets in above $x\approx0.76$ m.
